known_facts_book1: A well-known democrat ('le démoc'), the terror of respectable people, who has spent twenty years dipping his long red beard into the beer of every democratic café.
Inherited a comfortable fortune from his father, a former confectioner, and has largely eaten through it.
Believed himself appointed prefect after the 4 September revolution, but was turned away when he tried to take up the post.
Spent the lead-up to the invasion energetically organizing (largely useless) defenses: having trenches dug, young trees felled across roads, and traps set.
Plans to make himself useful at Le Havre, where new fortifications will be needed.
Offers his rum flask to the other coach passengers when hunger strikes; only Loiseau accepts.
Is the only traveler who accepts Boule de Suif's food as an equal without hesitation, alongside the two nuns.
Argues with Mme Follenvie that war is barbarous when attacking a peaceful neighbor but a sacred duty in self-defense, and calls her 'citoyenne' approvingly.
Refuses to go with the count and Carré-Lamadon to petition the Prussian officer, declaring he wants nothing to do with Germans.
Tries to seduce Boule de Suif at her door on the first night at the inn in Tôtes; she refuses him because Prussians are billeted in the next room, and he retreats after a single kiss.
Is caught spying on the same encounter by Loiseau, in reverse — he is himself the one Loiseau sees stealing to Boule de Suif's door.
Is the only traveler to openly condemn the group's campaign to pressure Boule de Suif, shouting 'Je vous dis à tous que vous venez de faire une infamie!' and storming out.
Whistles the Marseillaise obstinately, and at times sings its words, all the way to Dieppe once the coach resumes its journey — visibly needling the other, now-relieved travelers.

Does not share his own food (four hard-boiled eggs and bread) with Boule de Suif at the end, despite having condemned the others' treatment of her; nobody, including him, pays her any attention while she cries.

known_relations_book1.Boule de Suif: Tries to seduce her the first night, is refused, and is later the only traveler to call the group's treatment of her 'une infamie' — though he too ignores her tears at the story's end.
known_relations_book1.Loiseau: Spies on him at Boule de Suif's door and mocks him afterward as 'not much fun tonight'.
known_relations_book1.M. Carré-Lamadon et le comte de Bréville: Refuses to join them in petitioning the Prussian officer.
